newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope says Christmas marred by Holy Land tensions.
newsitem.headline: Pope says Christmas marred by Holy Land tensions.

text.p: Pope John Paul wished the world a happy Christmas in 55 languages on Wednesday but said the spirit of the nativity was marred by tensions in the Holy Land and international indifference to the tragedy in Africa.

In his "Urbi et Orbi" (to the city and the world) blessing and message, the 76-year-old Polish Pontiff said Christmas meant not being resigned to violence and injustice but striving to overcome hatred and rancour and returning to dialogue.
The Pontiff, who this year did not celebrate a Christmas day mass for health reasons, spoke to thousands of people gathered under dark skies in a rainy St Peter's Square.

After the address, the Pope, who appeared in relatively good form, delivered brief Christmas greetings in 55 languages, including Arabic, Hebrew, Tamil, Latin and his native Polish, and in languages spoken in Burundi and Rwanda.

"The echo of the songs of Christmas must travel much farther," he said, speaking from the central balcony of Christendom's largest Church. "It must resound beyond walls where the clash of arms is still heard, shattering the spell of peace brought by this holy day."

The Pope, celebrating his 19th Christmas season as leader of the world's 960 million Roman Catholics, said that while the past year had brought peace to Bosnia, Guatemala and elsewhere, it was sorely lacking in many other places.
"I am thinking of Bethlehem and all the Holy Land, where Jesus was born and lived: the land that he loved, the land where hope must not die, despite provocations and profound differences," he said.
Israel handed over Bethlehem and five other West Bank cities to the PLO last year under a self-rule deal that calls for a gradual end to nearly three decades of Israeli occupation.
But the Jewish state imposed a closure on the West Bank and Gaza after a spate of Islamic militant suicide bombings. Residents say the closure strangles the city's economy.

The Pope expressed his concern over a slowing of the Mideast peace process in talks with Palestinian president Yasser Arafat last week and is expected to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu next month.
He spoke of the "throes of unjustifiable violence" in Algeria, shaken by attacks by Islamic fundamentalists.
The Pontiff dedicated an entire section of his address to the seemingly endless tragedy of central Africa.

"And how can we forget Africa?," he asked. "At its very heart, in the region of the Great Lakes, this young continent is experiencing, amid the general indifference of the international community, one of the cruellest human tragedies of its history."
The Pope has made numerous appeals for a solution to the crisis of Rwanda, to which hundreds of thousands of refugees are returning after ethnic genocide in 1994.
"Thousands and thousands of people -- our brothers and sisters -- wander, displaced, victims of fear, hunger and disease. They, alas, will not be able to feel the joy of Christmas," he said.
"No one can remain indifferent before this scandal, which words and pictures can only faintly begin to describe," he said.
The Pope, who has suffered from a series of health problems in recent years, celebrated a solemn midnight mass in St Peter's Basilica 12 hours before his "Urbi et Orbi" address.
But, heeding medical advice to conserve his strength, he skipped the Christmas Day mass in the Basilica. The decison was announced by the Vatican two weeks ago.
The fact that the Pope missed one of the key celebrations of the Christian liturgical calendar again underscored that old age is taking its toll on his stamina.
Celebrating the day mass as well ast the midnight mass would have permitted the Pope -- an early riser -- very little rest.
When he left hospital in October after an appendix operation -- the last of a series of health problems -- doctors ordered him to rest more.
